claims.text: Microeconomics is the study of the economic choices of individual households, firms and particular markets, such as how one household divides its income or how one firm sets its price.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Questions about the price of one good, the output of one firm and the jobs of one firm's workers are microeconomic questions, because each concerns a single decision-maker or a single market.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: When Kaoko Juice of Opuwo weighs a price of N$14 against N$12 for its bottles, it faces a microeconomic choice, because the decision belongs to one firm selling in one market.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Macroeconomics is the study of the economy as a whole: total output of goods and services, the general level of prices and total employment.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Economy-wide indicators such as the rate at which consumer prices rise, the growth of total output and the share of the workforce without jobs are macroeconomic measures.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The test that separates a microeconomic question from a macroeconomic one is the level it sits at: a single household, firm or market is microeconomics, whereas an economy-wide total or average is macroeconomics.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Macroeconomic outcomes are built from many microeconomic decisions taken together, so a change at one firm can, when repeated across an economy, move economy-wide totals.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The decision makers studied in microeconomics are consumers or households, workers and producers or firms, each deciding for itself within particular markets: what to buy, where and how much to work, and what to produce and at what price.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The main decision makers in macroeconomics are the government, which decides taxation, public spending and borrowing for the whole economy, and the central bank, which decides interest rates and influences the money supply; international bodies such as the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank and the World Trade Organization also take decisions that affect whole economies.
